drafts.A: Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT) learn multimodal continuous behavior from uncurated datasets by predicting learned action tokens rather than k-means action bins. Residual vector quantization represents actions or action chunks through coarse and fine codes; a transformer predicts these codes from observation histories, optionally conditioned on goal observations, and a continuous offset refines the decoded actions. Token prediction produces actions in a single forward pass rather than through iterative denoising. Across simulated manipulation and locomotion tasks, VQ-BeT generally matches or exceeds the tested transformer and diffusion baselines, with subtask entropy and multimodal rollouts indicating diverse behavior. Diffusion policies nevertheless perform better on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. On a low-cost mobile manipulator under fully closed-loop control, the advantage is larger for sequential tasks: VQ-BeT completes 19/30 two-phase trials versus 11/30 for an adapted DiffusionPolicy-T, compared with 47/50 versus 45/50 single-phase trials. Onboard CPU inference takes 207.25 ms versus 5243.82 ms, reducing prediction cost when controller noise requires feedback at every policy step.
drafts.B: Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT) model multimodal robot behavior by learning action tokens from uncurated behavior data rather than assigning actions to k-means bins. Residual vector quantization encodes each action or action chunk with a coarse code followed by a code for the unrepresented embedding residual. A transformer predicts these codes from observation histories with optional goal conditioning; their vectors are summed, decoded, and refined by a continuous offset. Actions are thus generated in one forward pass rather than by iterative denoising. In simulated manipulation and locomotion, VQ-BeT generally matches or exceeds the tested baselines in task performance, while entropy measurements and rollouts show diverse behaviors; diffusion policies nevertheless lead on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. On a low-cost mobile manipulator, controller noise disrupts receding-horizon rollouts, so all policies are evaluated fully closed-loop. Single-phase totals are similar (47/50 versus 45/50), but VQ-BeT completes 19/30 two-phase trials versus 11/30 for an adapted DiffusionPolicy-T. Onboard CPU inference takes 207.25 ms versus 5243.82 ms, reducing the computational cost of generating a fresh action at every step.

drafts.A: The hardware comparison shows a larger aggregate success advantage for VQ-BeT on sequences than on standalone tasks. With fully closed-loop execution and ten trials per task, VQ-BeT and the adapted DiffusionPolicy-T complete 47/50 and 45/50 single-phase trials, respectively, compared with 19/30 and 11/30 two-phase trials. The aggregate gain does not extend to every sequence: on closing both doors, diffusion succeeds in 6/10 trials versus 5/10 for VQ-BeT, which nonetheless generates both possible closing orders. Final completion rates on each of four longer sequences are at least three times the baseline's. The timing comparison matters for this platform because controller noise disrupted receding-horizon rollouts, prompting action prediction at every step. On the robot's onboard CPU, average inference takes 207.25 ms for VQ-BeT versus 5243.82 ms for diffusion. Thus, higher aggregate sequence completion accompanies faster per-step prediction under the evaluated closed-loop protocol.
drafts.B: On the real robot, VQ-BeT's advantage over diffusion is larger for sequential tasks than for standalone tasks. With all policies run fully closed-loop, VQ-BeT and an adapted DiffusionPolicy-T complete 47/50 and 45/50 single-phase trials, respectively, but 19/30 and 11/30 two-phase trials. Across four longer sequences, VQ-BeT's final success rate is at least three times the diffusion baseline's, reinforcing the distinction between individual task execution and completing a sequence. VQ-BeT also closes the fridge and toaster in both orders, retaining alternative task sequences rather than a single rollout mode. The hardware makes inference cost consequential: controller noise disrupts short open-loop rollouts on the low-cost mobile manipulator, requiring a new policy prediction at every step. Onboard CPU inference takes 207.25 ms for VQ-BeT versus 5243.82 ms for diffusion, reducing the prediction cost of fully closed-loop execution.

drafts.A: Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT) model multimodal behavior using learned latent action tokens rather than clustering actions directly. Residual quantization combines coarse codes with finer corrections; a transformer predicts these codes from observation histories, optionally conditioned on goals, and an offset refines decoded actions. Action or action-chunk generation takes one forward pass, avoiding the iterative denoising used by diffusion policies. Across simulated manipulation and locomotion tasks, VQ-BeT combines competitive task performance with diverse behavior, although diffusion policies perform better on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. For each of four longer tasks, VQ-BeT also achieves at least three times the baseline's final success count. With all policies executed fully closed-loop, mean inference on an RTX A4000 is 18.06 ms versus 573.49 ms for the diffusion baseline. The real-robot comparison couples higher sequence-completion rates with lower action-generation time under per-step feedback.

drafts.A: In sparse-reward robot learning, imitation can supply candidate actions while an online actor is still ineffective. Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) keeps imitation and RL policies separate: a target critic selects between their proposals for both interaction and temporal-difference bootstrapping, greedily or by value-weighted sampling. The bootstrap target therefore evaluates the same hybrid selection rule used to collect experience, instead of relying on the RL actor alone. Policy separation also accommodates different architecture preferences observed in Robomimic: ResNet-18 performs better for cloning, whereas the proposed shallow vision-transformer architecture performs better in online RL. Actor dropout improves sample efficiency and also benefits regularized fine-tuning; retaining it does not prevent performance losses when either proposal mechanism is removed. IBRL outperforms demonstration oversampling and regularized fine-tuning on Robomimic, while performing similarly to fine-tuning on simpler Meta-World tasks. In real-robot cloth hanging with manual resets, 30 demonstrations and 30,000 interaction steps yield 85% success for IBRL versus 65% for cloning, 35% for fine-tuning, and 15% for oversampling, in 20 evaluation trials per method.
drafts.B: Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) uses a separately trained imitation policy to supply candidate actions for both online interaction and temporal-difference targets. An off-policy critic compares imitation and reinforcement-learning proposals when selecting actions and repeats this comparison when bootstrapping, extending the role of demonstrations beyond exploration without a behavior-cloning regularizer. Keeping the policies separate permits different visual architectures: comparisons favor ResNet-18 for cloning but a shallow vision transformer for online learning. Actor dropout further improves sample efficiency. Under sparse task-completion rewards, IBRL learns faster than demonstration oversampling and regularized fine-tuning on Robomimic, while regularized fine-tuning performs similarly on simpler Meta-World tasks. Removing either proposal mechanism reduces performance despite retaining actor dropout, supporting their complementary roles in interaction and value learning. On real robots with manual resets, IBRL uses 30 demonstrations and 30,000 interaction steps to achieve 85% cloth-hanging success, compared with 65% for the reference cloning policy, 35% for regularized fine-tuning, and 15% for demonstration oversampling. Only IBRL exceeds cloning on this task within the tested interaction budget.

drafts.A: On the deformable-cloth Hang task, IBRL improves on the reference imitation policy, whereas both alternative demonstration-assisted RL methods finish below it. Each RL method uses 30 demonstrations and 30,000 interaction steps; final-checkpoint success is 85% for IBRL, 35% for regularized fine-tuning, and 15% for RLPD, versus 65% for the demonstration-trained cloning policy. These final-checkpoint evaluations use 20 trials per method with shared initial conditions, yielding a 20-percentage-point improvement over cloning. The hardware protocol uses sparse success rewards and manual resets. Complementary Robomimic Square ablations show that actor dropout improves the baselines without closing the gap to IBRL; removing either imitation-based action proposal or bootstrap proposal degrades IBRL even with dropout retained. The ablations support both proposal mechanisms beyond actor regularization, while Hang documents improvement over the reference policy within the hardware budget.
drafts.B: On the real-world Hang task, IBRL improves on its imitation reference where alternative demonstration-based RL methods fall below cloning. With 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online interaction steps, IBRL achieves 85% success, versus 65% for the cloning reference, 35% for regularized fine-tuning (RFT), and 15% for demonstration oversampling (RLPD). Final checkpoints are evaluated over 20 trials per method using the same initial conditions; the hardware protocol uses sparse success rewards and manual resets. The 20-percentage-point gain over cloning measures policy improvement on deformable-cloth manipulation. Robomimic Square ablations distinguish this benefit from actor regularization alone: removing either imitation-based action proposal or bootstrap proposal reduces performance with dropout retained, and dropout-enhanced baselines remain below IBRL. Together, these comparisons support retaining imitation as a source of candidate actions during both interaction and target computation, rather than relying only on regularization or demonstration replay.

drafts.A: Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) uses a separately trained imitation policy to guide sparse-reward robot learning without imposing an imitation loss on the RL actor. A critic selects the higher-valued imitation or RL action both during interaction and when constructing temporal-difference targets, aligning bootstrapping with the hybrid interaction policy. Keeping the policies separate permits different imitation and RL encoders; actor dropout and a shallow vision-transformer critic further improve pixel-based learning. IBRL matches regularized fine-tuning on simpler Meta-World tasks and outperforms fine-tuning and demonstration oversampling on harder Robomimic tasks. Hardware training uses sparse success rewards and manual resets. Removing either imitation proposal degrades performance even with actor dropout, supporting the contribution of imitation in both interaction and value-target computation.

With 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online interaction steps, IBRL achieves 85% success, compared with 65% for behavior cloning (BC), 35% for regularized fine-tuning (RFT), and 15% for demonstration oversampling (RLPD). drafts.B: On cloth hanging, IBRL improves on the imitation reference, whereas regularized fine-tuning (RFT) and demonstration oversampling (RLPD) achieve lower success than that reference.
